translationRepairs.before: After Murong Bao succeeded, he appointed Murong De as commissioner bearing credentials, area commander-in-chief of military affairs in six provinces Ji, Yan, Qing, Xu, Jing, and Yu, specially advanced, chariot and cavalry general-in-chief, governor of Ji, concurrently colonel of the Southern Man, stationed at Ye, abolished the rear headquarters, and used the area command to oversee the southern summer in full.
translationRepairs.after: After Murong Bao succeeded, he appointed Murong De as commissioner bearing credentials, area commander-in-chief of military affairs in the six provinces Ji, Yan, Qing, Xu, Jing, and Yu, specially advanced, chariot-and-cavalry general-in-chief, governor of Ji, concurrently colonel of the Southern Man, stationed at Ye; he abolished the rear headquarters and used the area command to oversee the southern Xia domains in full.
translationRepairs.reason: 南夏 denotes the southern Xia, meaning the southern Chinese domains; translating 夏 as the season 'summer' is nonsensical in this jurisdictional context.

translationRepairs.before: When Chui succeeded the throne, he was changed to Prince of Fanyang, gradually promoted prefect of Wei, with addition of regular attendant for scattered cavalry.
translationRepairs.after: When Chui succeeded the throne, [De] was changed to Prince of Fanyang, gradually promoted to Yin of Wei (capital-region prefect), and given the additional title of Cavalier Regular Attendant.
translationRepairs.reason: The silent subject remains Murong De, and 魏尹 is the capital-region office Yin of Wei rather than a generic prefecture. The proposal restores both points.

translationRepairs.before: After Murong Chui’s rebellion collapsed he was deported to Chang’an, where Fu Jian named him prefect of Zhangye; a few years later he was sent home in disgrace.
translationRepairs.after: After Murong Chui’s defeat he was moved to Chang’an, where Fu Jian named him prefect of Zhangye; a few years later he was dismissed and sent home.
translationRepairs.reason: 垂敗 says that Chui was defeated; it does not characterize the event as a collapsed rebellion. 免歸 directly states dismissal and return, without the added claim that the return was disgraceful.

translationRepairs.before: Ding Tong, chief clerk under Tuoba Zhang, defected with his troops and reported that Zhang's army was exhausted and vulnerable.
translationRepairs.after: Ding Jian, chief clerk under Tuoba Zhang, defected with his troops and reported that Zhang's army was exhausted and vulnerable.
translationRepairs.reason: The source explicitly names 丁建, Ding Jian. Ding Tong is a different person who appears later in the chapter and should not be substituted here.

translationRepairs.before: Tuoba Zhang's chief clerk Ding Tong led his masses to surrender and said Tuoba Zhang's army was worn and could be defeated.
translationRepairs.after: Tuoba Zhang's chief clerk Ding Jian led his masses to surrender and said Tuoba Zhang's army was worn and could be defeated.
translationRepairs.reason: The literal field repeats the same confusion of 丁建 with the later Ding Tong. Ding Jian is the only name attested in this sentence.

translationRepairs.before: Before long Murong Bao made Murong De chancellor and governor of Ji, with delegated authority over the southern summer.
translationRepairs.after: Before long Murong Bao made Murong De chancellor and governor of Ji, with delegated authority over the southern Xia domains.
translationRepairs.reason: As in the earlier appointment, 南夏 denotes the southern Xia domains under delegated authority, not 'southern summer.'

translationRepairs.before: Murong De sent Central Army Murong Fa and Pacification General Murong He to meet them, and the Jin army was routed.
translationRepairs.after: Murong De sent the Central Army commander Murong Fa, the Pacification General Murong He, and others to resist them, and the Jin army was routed.
translationRepairs.reason: The source lists Murong Fa, Murong He, and others (等), and uses 距 in the sense of resisting the Jin force. The proposal restores the omitted collective and clarifies the offices.

translationRepairs.before: We should send eloquent men ahead to persuade, then follow with a great army; Bi Lü Hun once betrayed the state's grace and is sure to turn toward civilization.
translationRepairs.after: We should send eloquent men ahead to persuade them, then follow with a great army; Pilü Hun, who once betrayed the state's grace, is sure to turn toward civilization.
translationRepairs.reason: The official's standard name is 辟閭渾, romanized Pilü Hun: Pilü is the compound surname and Hun the given name. The chapter's 避閭渾 is a textual variant, not a basis for the split and misread 'Bi Lü Hun.'

translationRepairs.before: In the fourth year he took the imperial title at the southern altar, amnestied the realm, adopted the Jianping era, placed a mobile temple south of the palace, and dispatched envoys to announce the deed.
translationRepairs.after: In Long'an 4 (AD 400), he claimed the imperial title at the southern suburban altar, issued a general amnesty, inaugurated the Jianping era, established a traveling ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys bearing the accession proclamation.
translationRepairs.reason: The narrative's fourth year is Long'an 4 (AD 400), when Murong De inaugurated Jianping. The revision preserves the source's disapproving 僭 with 'claimed' and makes the date and accession sequence explicit.

translationRepairs.before: At that time Huan Xuan's general was about to usurp and killed those who would not attach to him.
translationRepairs.after: At that time Huan Xuan was about to carry out usurpation and killed those who would not attach to him.
translationRepairs.reason: 將行篡逆 takes Huan Xuan as its subject: he was about to usurp. Treating 將 as the noun 'general' invents another actor and corrupts the syntax.

translationRepairs.before: When news came of Huan Xuan's fall Murong De mobilized then canceled the campaign because of illness.
translationRepairs.after: Soon they heard Huan Xuan was defeated; Murong De made Murong Zhen the vanguard and Murong Zhong supreme commander, assigning twenty thousand foot and five thousand horse with a set departure date, but Murong De fell ill and therefore halted the army.
translationRepairs.reason: The existing idiomatic sentence drops the named vanguard and commander, the assigned infantry and cavalry, and the fixed departure date. The proposal accurately restores those material details before Murong De's illness halted the expedition.

translationRepairs.before: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou closed Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
translationRepairs.after: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou raised a mound over Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
translationRepairs.reason: The Jin shu states that King Wu acted on Bi Gan's tomb; the parallel Shiji Music Treatise preserves Zheng Xuan's gloss that this was heaping earth. The revised wording expresses that sense without adding a date or physical details.

translationRepairs.before: They ran decoy coffers out each gate and hid his true burial in the hills.
translationRepairs.after: That night they prepared more than ten coffins and sent them out through the four gates, burying him secretly in the mountain valleys; in the end, no one knew where his body lay.
translationRepairs.reason: 十餘棺 specifies over ten coffins; 夜, 分出四門, 潛葬山谷 and 竟不知其屍之所在 provide the night, four gates, concealed burial and unknown resting place. The suggested wording restores these details without inventing an identified decoy coffin.

translationRepairs.before: He was posthumously titled Emperor Xianwu.
translationRepairs.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
translationRepairs.reason: 偽 expresses the source's judgment of illegitimacy, while 諡 is a posthumous title. Avoid 'the Jin historian': the Book of Jin is a later compilation, so that label misleadingly suggests an author from the Jin period. The wording attributes the judgment to this history rather than endorsing it.

translationRepairs.before: His temple posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu.
translationRepairs.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
translationRepairs.reason: 諡 is the posthumous designation, not a temple name. 偽 expresses this history's claim of illegitimacy; the proposed 'Jin historian' risks misidentifying the compiler's period. Zizhi Tongjian 114 separately distinguishes 諡獻武皇帝 from 廟號世宗.

translationRepairs.before: In the fourth year he usurped the emperor's title at the southern suburb, issued a general amnesty, changed the era name to Jianping, set a traveling temple south of the palace, and sent envoys with the document to report completion.
translationRepairs.after: In the fourth year, at the southern suburb he assumed the imperial throne—an act the history presents as usurpation—issued a general amnesty, changed the era name to Jianping, established a temporary ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys bearing a document to report the accomplishment there.
translationRepairs.reason: Revise to restore the locative 焉, read as the immediately preceding temporary temple; this antecedent is plausible but interpretative. Attribute the evaluative 僭 to the history, not objective fact. Keep the document and reported accomplishment unspecified. The AD conversion in the idiomatic field remains unaudited.

translationRepairs.before: Thereupon he took Yan Mo along to the temple of Prince Jing of Chengyang at Hancheng, feasted the common elders at Shen Pool, climbed north Mount Sheshou, looked east at the tripod legs of terrain, then gazed at Mount Niu and sighed, saying, 'From antiquity there has been no not dying!'
translationRepairs.after: Thereupon he took Yan Mo along to the temple of Han Prince Jing of Chengyang, feasted the common elders at Shen Pool, climbed north Mount Sheshou, looked east at the tripod legs of terrain, then gazed at Mount Niu and sighed, saying, 'From antiquity there has been no not dying!'

translationRepairs.before: He opened ironworks on Mount Shang and salt monopolies at Wuchang Marsh to swell the army's coffers.
translationRepairs.after: He established smelting works on Mount Shang and a salt office at Wuchang Marsh to increase resources for the army and the state.
translationRepairs.reason: 冶 does not specify iron, 鹽官 is a salt office, and 軍國 includes military and state use; the existing idiom adds unsupported details.

translationRepairs.before: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall and hid him in a forward lodging.
translationRepairs.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.
translationRepairs.reason: 遜進 is the attendant’s name and 進舍 his residence; the understood subject of hiding is plausibly De, the person rescued.

translationRepairs.before: A eunuch helped Murong De over the wall into hiding.
translationRepairs.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.
translationRepairs.reason: 遜進 is the attendant’s name and 進舍 his residence; the understood subject of hiding is plausibly De, the person rescued.

translationRepairs.before: Spanning several thousand li, hosts exceeding a hundred thousand, we could west merge with strong Qin and north resist Great Wei.
translationRepairs.after: Spanning several thousand li with a host exceeding a hundred thousand, we could annex strong Qin to the west and resist Great Wei to the north.
translationRepairs.reason: 西並強秦 describes expansion by absorbing Qin to the west, in contrast with resistance to Wei to the north.

translationRepairs.before: He staged a review west of the city with hundreds of thousands on parade.
translationRepairs.after: He reviewed his forces west of the city: 370,000 infantry, 17,000 vehicles, and 53,000 armored cavalry. They stretched across the mountains and marshes, their banners filled the landscape, and the sound of gongs and drums shook heaven and earth.
translationRepairs.reason: The figures and the mountain, banner, gong, and drum imagery are explicitly present; these are reported figures, not verified headcounts.

translationRepairs.before: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke avenged Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
translationRepairs.after: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke took vengeance on Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
translationRepairs.reason: In 仇齊 Qi is the object of Xi Ke’s hostility, as 楚 is the object of Zixu’s resentment, not the party he avenged.

translationRepairs.before: Murong Chao, whom he had summoned from Chang'an, now arrived.
translationRepairs.after: De's nephew Murong Chao, whom De had earlier sought to bring from Chang'an, now arrived.
translationRepairs.reason: 兄子 identifies Chao as De’s elder brother’s son. 迎 does not by itself establish the precise means, so the narrower reviewed wording avoids asserting a summons.

translationRepairs.before: He named Murong Chao crown prince and issued a broad amnesty.
translationRepairs.after: He issued an edict naming Murong Chao crown prince and granting a general amnesty throughout the realm; sons succeeding their fathers were each granted two grades of rank.
translationRepairs.reason: 子為父後者人爵二級 grants two grades to sons succeeding their fathers; an increase would imply an existing rank that the wording does not require.

translationRepairs.before: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I reverently face south to court the lords; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
translationRepairs.after: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I conduct myself respectfully, face south, and receive the lords at court; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
translationRepairs.reason: The south-facing ruler receives the lords at court; the former English reverses their relationship. This is a focused correction and does not approve every inherited phrase.

translationRepairs.before: Earlier, De had welcomed his brother's son Chao from Chang'an; at this point he arrived.
translationRepairs.after: Earlier, De had sought to bring his brother's son Chao from Chang'an; at this point Chao arrived.
translationRepairs.reason: The earlier 迎 action precedes Chao's arrival. 'Sought to bring' is interpretive: 迎 may mean to go meet or fetch, and the precise method and any unsuccessful attempt are not established.

translationRepairs.before: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince, amnestied the realm, and for sons continuing fathers raised each man's rank two grades.
translationRepairs.after: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince and granting an amnesty throughout the realm; sons succeeding their fathers were each granted two grades of rank.
translationRepairs.reason: The text grants qualifying sons two grades of rank without explicitly asserting that each previously held a rank; this aligns the literal with the reviewed idiomatic field.

translationRepairs.before: Duan Hong and the rest heard the alarm and sealed the four gates with troops.
translationRepairs.after: Duan Hong and the others heard of the palace disturbance and stationed their troops at the four gates.
translationRepairs.reason: The palace disturbance prompts Duan Hong and others to deploy troops at the four gates; the Chinese does not explicitly say the gates were sealed. This narrow proposal leaves the muster or command nuance of 勒兵 implicit.

translationRepairs.before: Murong De re-entered the palace, executed Hou Chimei's faction, and Murong Da fled to Wei.
translationRepairs.after: Murong De entered the palace and executed Hou Chimei and the others; Murong Da fled in fear to Wei.
translationRepairs.reason: De enters the palace and executes Chimei and others; Da flees to Wei in fear. The expanded names Hou Chimei and Murong Da are given in the preceding context, s0212.
